intro: Dig a hole in a backyard almost anywhere in central Illinois and the dirt comes up black. That black soil is the reason for nearly everything else in this unit: the farms, the towns, the railroads, and the city of Chicago. It was made by giant sheets of ice and by thousands of years of tall prairie grass. To understand Illinois, you start with the land.

Then you meet the people. A city of earthen mounds a thousand years ago. Native nations who gave the state its name. French traders in canoes. Settlers on flatboats, Irish canal diggers, railroad builders, and families who came north on the train to find work and freedom. A fire that burned a city to the ground, and the people who built it back taller.

By the end of this unit you will be able to read a map of Illinois and explain its rivers, regions and weather. You will be able to tell how the land got so flat and so rich. And you will be able to tell the story of how a quiet prairie became a state of nearly thirteen million people, using evidence: a map, a number, a journal, a photograph.
bigQuestion: How have the land of Illinois and the people of Illinois shaped each other?

timeline.t: The last glaciers melt back from northern Illinois, leaving flat land and crushed rock.
Cahokia, the largest city north of Mexico, is at its busiest near the Mississippi.
Marquette and Jolliet paddle the Mississippi and Illinois rivers and meet the Illinois people.
Illinois becomes the twenty-first state, with its capital at Kaskaskia.
John Deere makes a steel plow that cuts through prairie sod; Chicago becomes a city.
The Illinois and Michigan Canal opens, linking Lake Michigan to the Illinois River.
The Illinois Central Railroad is finished, the longest railroad in the world at the time.
Abraham Lincoln leaves Springfield to become president.
The Great Chicago Fire burns for two days; the city begins to rebuild at once.
Jane Addams opens Hull House on Halsted Street in Chicago.
The Great Migration brings hundreds of thousands of Black Americans to Chicago.
Barack Obama, a senator from Illinois, is elected president and speaks in Grant Park.

a huge, thick sheet of ice that moves slowly over the land
a wide, open land of tall grasses and wildflowers with few trees
the dark top layer of earth where plants grow best
an area of land whose parts share something, like a kind of land or way of life
something from nature that people use, like soil, water or coal
a spinning funnel of wind that drops from a storm cloud
a hill of earth built by people, used for temples, homes or burials
the exchange of animal furs for goods like metal tools and cloth
a long, narrow waterway dug by people so boats can travel on it
a person who moves to a new country to live
the move of millions of Black Americans from the South to northern cities in the 1900s

test.q: Which river forms the western border of Illinois?
test.why: The Mississippi runs down the whole west side of the state.

test.q: Which state is south of Illinois, across the Ohio River?
test.why: Kentucky lies south of Illinois across the Ohio River.

test.q: Why is most of Illinois flat?
choices: Glaciers scraped it flat during the Ice Age
test.why: Ice sheets more than a mile thick ground down hills and filled valleys, then left crushed rock behind.

test.q: Which part of Illinois did the glaciers NOT flatten?
choices: The Shawnee Hills in the far south
test.why: The ice never reached the southern tip, so the Shawnee Hills are still rough and rocky.

test.q: What made the topsoil of Illinois so deep and black?
choices: Thousands of years of prairie grass rotting into the ground
test.why: Prairie plants and their deep roots died and regrew for thousands of years.

test.q: What are the two main crops of Illinois?
test.why: Corn and soybeans cover most of the farmland in the state.

test.q: What happens when warm, wet air from the Gulf meets cold, dry air from the north over Illinois?
test.why: The clash of the two air masses can twist into a spinning funnel of wind.

test.q: What did Chicago do to its river in 1900?
choices: Made it flow backward, away from the lake
test.why: Engineers reversed the river so the city's waste would not flow into its drinking water.

choices: A great mound city near the Mississippi around the year 1100
test.why: Cahokia held ten to twenty thousand people and more than a hundred earthen mounds.

test.q: Where does the name Illinois come from?
choices: The Illinois people, a group of Native nations
test.why: The French wrote down the name of the Illinois nations, and the land took that name.

test.q: Why did French traders come to Illinois?
test.why: Beaver fur made expensive hats in Europe, and traders exchanged metal goods and cloth for it.

test.q: What did the Illinois and Michigan Canal and the railroads do for Chicago?
choices: They moved the capital to Chicago
They made Chicago the trading center between East and West
test.why: Goods from farms and forests flowed through Chicago to markets in the East, and the city boomed.

test.q: How did Chicago change after the fire of 1871?
choices: It rebuilt with brick, stone and steel and grew into a great city
test.why: New laws banned wooden downtown buildings, builders invented the skyscraper, and by 1890 the city had a million people.

test.q: Why did many Black families leave the South for Chicago in the early 1900s?
choices: For jobs, schools and the right to vote
test.why: Southern laws denied Black people votes, good schools and good jobs, while northern factories needed workers.

test.q: Which Illinoisan wrote the truth about lynching and helped found civil rights groups?
test.why: Ida B. Wells, a journalist who moved to Chicago in the 1890s, reported on lynching at great risk to her life.

write.prompt: Make a claim: Which shaped Illinois more, its land or its people? Support your claim with at least three pieces of evidence from this unit, such as the glaciers and soil, the rivers and canals, the fire and rebuilding, or the Great Migration.
tips: Claim: choose land or people, and say it in one clear sentence.
Evidence: use specific facts, like the depth of the topsoil, the year the canal opened, or how many people lived in Chicago before and after the fire.
Reasoning: explain how each piece of evidence connects to your claim, not just what happened.
The other side: name one strong fact that supports the opposite claim, and explain why your claim still holds.
End with one sentence about what your answer means for Illinois today.

title: Illinois: Land and People

chapters.title: The Prairie State
chapters.bigQuestion: How did the land of Illinois get the way it is, and how do people use it?

story.title: Grass Taller Than You
story.kicker: Step into a restored prairie in June. The grass closes over your head, and the sky goes away.
paragraphs: It is a hot morning in June. A fourth-grade class steps off a bus at a nature preserve an hour from Chicago. A ranger leads them down a mowed path. On both sides, grass rises higher and higher. By the middle of the path, the tallest kids cannot see over it. The grass is called big bluestem. By August it will stand eight feet tall.

The ranger stops. She tells the class to be quiet and listen. Bees hum. A red-winged blackbird calls from a stalk. The wind moves through the grass and makes a sound like the ocean. Purple flowers called coneflowers poke up between the blades. Nobody planted them. They grew here on their own.

Then the ranger says something surprising. Two hundred years ago, most of Illinois looked like this. Not corn. Not soybeans. Not streets and houses. Grass and flowers, from horizon to horizon, taller than a person on a horse. Travelers wrote that they felt like they were sailing on a green sea.

Today almost all of that prairie is gone. Farmers plowed it up because the soil under it was some of the richest on Earth. That soil still feeds the state and much of the world. This small patch was saved and replanted so people could see what the land used to be. The ranger asks the class to look down at the dirt. It is nearly black.

That black dirt is the reason Illinois is called the Prairie State. It is the reason for the farms, the towns, the railroads, and in a way, the city of Chicago. To understand Illinois, you have to start with the land.
story.think: If you could see Illinois from an airplane two hundred years ago and today, what would look different? What might look the same?

lessons.title: Neighbors and Borders
lessons.mainIdea: Illinois sits in the middle of the country, with five neighbor states and a Great Lake around it.
reading: Find Illinois on a map of the United States. It is near the center of the country, in the region called the Midwest. It is shaped a little like a long arrowhead pointing south. From the top of the state to the bottom is about 380 miles. That is a long drive, more than six hours on the highway.

Illinois has five *neighbor* states. Wisconsin is to the north. Iowa and Missouri are to the west. Kentucky is to the south. Indiana is to the east. A line where one state ends and another begins is called a *border*. Some of these borders are straight lines drawn on paper. Others follow rivers.

In the northeast corner, Illinois touches Lake Michigan. Across the lake is the state of Michigan. Chicago, the biggest city in Illinois, sits on the lake shore. The capital, where the state government works, is Springfield, near the middle of the state.

words.d: a state, town or person right next to you
the line where one state or country ends and another begins
the city where a state's or country's government works

look.title: The Shape of the State
look.text: Look at a map of Illinois. Trace the east side with your finger. The top part is a straight line. Then, partway down, the line starts to wiggle. Now trace the whole west side. It wiggles the entire way. The wiggles are rivers.
look.prompt: Why might some borders be straight and others wiggle?

check.q: What is the capital of Illinois?
check.why: Springfield, near the middle of the state, is where the state government works. Chicago is the biggest city but not the capital.

check.q: What is a border?
choices: The line where one state ends and another begins
The biggest city in a state
check.why: A border is the dividing line between two states or countries. Some are straight, some follow rivers.

check.q: About how far is it from the top of Illinois to the bottom?
check.why: The state is about 380 miles long from north to south, more than six hours of driving.

lessons.title: Rivers That Draw the Lines
lessons.mainIdea: Great rivers form most of the borders of Illinois and carry its goods to the sea.
reading: The wiggly borders of Illinois are rivers. The *Mississippi River* runs down the whole west side of the state. It separates Illinois from Iowa and Missouri. It is one of the longest rivers in the world. Farmers have shipped corn down the Mississippi on boats for two hundred years. At the very bottom of the state, at the town of Cairo, the Ohio River joins it.

The *Ohio River* forms the southern border with Kentucky. The Wabash River forms the lower part of the eastern border with Indiana. Before there were roads or trains, rivers were the highways. A flatboat could float a family and everything they owned downstream.

One big river runs through the middle of the state instead of around it. The *Illinois River* starts near Chicago and flows southwest across the state to the Mississippi. Long ago, Native people, French traders and settlers all used it as a path. Today barges still carry grain, coal and steel on it.

words.d: the huge river that forms the western border of Illinois
the river that forms the southern border of Illinois
the river that flows across the middle of the state to the Mississippi
a long, flat boat that carries heavy loads like grain or coal

look.title: Rivers of Illinois, Roughly
look.cite: U.S. Geological Survey, standard rounded lengths
look.prompt: Which river is the longest? Which of these four rivers stays mostly inside Illinois?

check.q: Where does the Ohio River join the Mississippi?
choices: At Cairo, at the bottom of the state
check.why: The two great rivers meet at the southern tip of Illinois, at the town of Cairo.

check.q: Why were rivers so important before roads and trains?
choices: They were the highways for moving people and goods
They had no fish in them
check.why: A boat could float a family or a load of corn downstream long before there were roads.

check.q: Which river flows through the middle of the state instead of around it?
check.why: The Illinois River starts near Chicago and crosses the state to the Mississippi. The other three are border rivers.

lessons.title: Lake Michigan
lessons.mainIdea: Lake Michigan gives Chicago its drinking water, its harbor and its cool breezes.
reading: Stand on the shore in Chicago and look east. You cannot see the other side. Lake Michigan is so big that it looks like an ocean, but the water is fresh, not salty. It is one of the five *Great Lakes*, which together hold about one fifth of all the fresh surface water on Earth. Illinois touches only Lake Michigan, along a short strip of shore in the northeast corner.

The lake is why Chicago is where it is. Ships carried goods from the East across the lakes. They unloaded them at Chicago. From there, the goods went by canal or train to the rest of the country. The lake is also where Chicago gets its drinking water. Big water plants clean it and pipe it to millions of homes.

The lake changes the weather too. In summer, a breeze off the cold water cools the lakefront. In winter, air blowing across the lake picks up moisture and drops heavy *lake-effect snow* on towns downwind. Illinois built parks and beaches along much of the shore so everyone can reach the water.

words.d: five huge freshwater lakes between the United States and Canada
water that is not salty, the kind people can drink
heavy snow made when cold air picks up moisture from a lake

look.title: A Cold Morning by the Lake
look.text: It is a June morning in Chicago. At a school ten miles from the lake, kids are in shorts and it is 80 degrees. At a school one block from the lake, kids are wearing sweatshirts and it is 65 degrees. A cool wind is blowing in from the water.
look.prompt: Why is it so much cooler near the lake? What do you think happens on a cold winter day?

check.q: Where does Chicago get its drinking water?
check.why: Water plants clean lake water and pipe it to millions of homes.

check.q: Why did the lake help Chicago grow?
choices: The lake was good for swimming
The lake made the land flat
Ships could unload goods there and send them on by canal or train
check.why: Chicago became a meeting point for ships from the East and trains and canals heading west.

check.q: What causes lake-effect snow?
choices: Cold air picking up moisture as it crosses the lake
Snow falling from the lake bottom
check.why: Cold winter air blows across the lake, picks up moisture and drops it as snow on towns downwind.

lessons.title: Ice Flattens the Land
lessons.mainIdea: Giant sheets of ice called glaciers scraped most of Illinois flat and left behind rich, crushed rock.
reading: Why is Illinois so flat? The answer is ice. Long ago, during the *Ice Age*, the Earth was colder than it is now. Snow piled up in Canada year after year and never melted. It squeezed into ice sheets more than a mile thick. Those ice sheets, called *glaciers*, slowly crept south like frozen bulldozers.

The glaciers pushed into Illinois more than once. The last big ice sheet melted away from northern Illinois roughly fifteen thousand years ago. As the ice moved, it scraped off hills. It filled in valleys. It ground rocks into fine dust. When it melted, it left that ground-up rock spread across the land. How do we know? The rocks and gravel under Illinois soil match rocks from Canada.

Not every part of the state was covered. The ice never reached the far south. So the Shawnee Hills there are still rough and rocky. A small corner in the northwest was also missed. It has steep hills too. Everywhere else, the glaciers left flat land. They also left a deep layer of crushed rock. That layer would become some of the best soil in the world.

words.d: a long time when Earth was colder and ice covered much of the land
a huge, thick sheet of ice that moves slowly over the land

look.title: High and Low Points of Illinois
look.prompt: The highest and lowest points are less than 1,000 feet apart. What does that tell you about the shape of the state?

check.q: What flattened most of Illinois?
choices: Glaciers, huge sheets of moving ice
check.why: During the Ice Age, thick ice sheets scraped the land flat and ground up the rocks.

check.q: How do we know glaciers came from the north?
choices: Rocks under Illinois soil match rocks from Canada
check.why: The crushed rock the ice left behind matches rock from far to the north, where the ice started.

check.q: Why are the Shawnee Hills in the south still rough and rocky?
choices: The glaciers never reached that far south
The glaciers pushed the hills up
check.why: The ice stopped before the far south. The hills there were never scraped flat.

lessons.title: Grass, Roots and Black Soil
lessons.mainIdea: Thousands of years of prairie grass built the deep black soil that makes Illinois farmland so rich.
reading: After the ice melted, grass grew on the crushed rock. Not short lawn grass. Tallgrass *prairie*: big bluestem, Indian grass and switchgrass, along with hundreds of kinds of wildflowers. The roots went deep, sometimes ten feet or more. Every year the grass died back and rotted. Every year the roots grew again. Fires set by lightning, and by Native people, burned off the dead stalks and kept trees from taking over.

This went on for thousands of years. All that rotting grass and root built up a thick layer of dark, crumbly earth called *topsoil*. In some places the black topsoil in Illinois is more than three feet deep. Rich soil is why the state's nickname is the Prairie State. It is also why Illinois grows so much food.

Settlers arrived in the early 1800s. Prairie then covered about two thirds of Illinois. Their iron plows stuck in the tough roots. Then, in 1837, a blacksmith named John Deere made a smooth steel plow. He worked in Grand Detour, Illinois. His plow cut clean through the sod. Within a few decades, nearly all the prairie was plowed into farms. Today less than one percent of the original prairie is left, in small preserves.

words.d: a wide, open land of tall grasses and wildflowers with few trees
the dark top layer of earth where plants grow best
the top layer of soil held together by grass roots

look.title: A Visitor Sees the Prairie, 1842
look.text: The English writer Charles Dickens visited a prairie in Illinois in 1842. He wrote that the grass stretched to the edge of the sky in every direction, with the sun setting on it like the sun over the sea, and that it was lonely and wild and huge. He admitted that he had expected to feel more amazed than he did.
look.prompt: Dickens compared the prairie to the sea. What do a prairie and an ocean have in common?

check.q: Why did fires help the prairie?
choices: They killed all the grass forever
They burned dead stalks and kept trees from taking over
check.why: Fires cleared the dead grass and stopped forests from growing. The deep roots survived and the prairie grew back.

check.q: Why did John Deere's steel plow matter?
choices: It was the first plow ever made
It could plant corn by itself
It cut through tough prairie roots that stuck iron plows
check.why: The smooth steel plow cut clean through the thick sod, so settlers could turn prairie into farms.

check.q: How much of the original Illinois prairie is left today?
check.why: Nearly all the prairie was plowed into farms. Only small preserves remain.

lessons.title: Chicago and the North
lessons.mainIdea: Northern Illinois holds Chicago and most of the state's people, jobs and factories.
reading: Geographers divide Illinois into *regions*, areas that share a way of life or a kind of land. The northern region is where most people live. About two out of every three Illinoisans live in Chicago and its suburbs, which spread across several counties. Chicago itself has about 2.7 million people, more than any other city in the Midwest.

Trains, highways and two big airports meet in Chicago. Factories, banks, hospitals and offices give people jobs. Rockford, in the north, makes machine parts and tools. Farther west, the Rock River winds through hilly country. The northwest corner, near Galena, has the highest ground in the state.

Northern Illinois is not all city. Just outside the *suburbs*, the land turns quickly to corn and soybean fields. Many towns are a mix: a train station to the city on one side, a grain elevator on the other.

words.d: an area of land whose parts share something, like a kind of land or way of life
a town just outside a big city where many people live and travel into the city

look.title: Biggest Cities in Illinois, About 2020
look.prompt: How many times bigger is Chicago than the next biggest city? Which cities on this list are suburbs of Chicago?

check.q: What is a region?
choices: An area whose parts share something, like the land or way of life
check.why: Geographers group land into regions that share features, such as flat farmland or a big city area.

check.q: Which of these is a job center in the north?
check.why: Rockford, in northern Illinois, is known for making machine parts and tools.

check.q: What would you likely see just outside the Chicago suburbs?
check.why: The land turns quickly from suburbs to farmland. Many towns have both a train station and a grain elevator.

lessons.title: Farmland and the Shawnee Hills
lessons.mainIdea: Central Illinois is flat farmland, while the far south rises into rocky, forested hills.
reading: Drive south from Chicago and the land opens up. Central Illinois is the flattest, richest farmland in the state. Fields of corn and soybeans run to the horizon. Farmhouses, grain silos and small towns break them up. Springfield, the capital, sits here. So does Peoria, on the Illinois River. So do Champaign and Urbana, home of the state's biggest university.

Keep driving south and the land changes. The glaciers never reached the bottom of the state, so the ground begins to roll and then rise. The *Shawnee Hills* cross southern Illinois from river to river. They are covered by the Shawnee National Forest, with sandstone cliffs, canyons and waterfalls. Some people call this region Little Egypt, and the town at the very tip is named Cairo.

Southern Illinois has a milder, wetter climate. Peach and apple orchards grow well. Coal lies under much of the region. Because the south and the north are so different, people from the two ends of the state sometimes feel like they live in different places. In a way, they do.

words.d: the rocky, forested hills across the far southern part of Illinois
a tall round tower where farmers store grain
a field of fruit trees

look.title: Two Postcards
look.text: Postcard one shows a field so flat that a grain elevator ten miles away looks close. The sky takes up most of the picture. Postcard two shows a hiker on a sandstone cliff above a green forest, with a creek far below. Both were mailed from Illinois.
look.prompt: Which region is each postcard from? What clue tells you?

check.q: What is central Illinois mostly used for?
check.why: Central Illinois has the flattest, richest farmland in the state.

check.q: Why is the far south of Illinois hilly?
choices: The glaciers did not reach that far, so nothing flattened it
The rivers pushed the land up
check.why: The ice sheets stopped before the southern tip. The old hills there were never scraped down.

check.q: Which crop grows well in the milder south?
check.why: Southern Illinois has a milder, wetter climate, which suits fruit orchards.

lessons.title: Seasons, Storms and Floods
lessons.mainIdea: Illinois has hot summers, cold winters and dangerous tornadoes and floods.
reading: Illinois is far from any ocean, so nothing keeps its weather steady. Summers are hot and sticky. Winters are cold, with snow that can shut down roads. Spring and fall bring quick changes. This pattern is called a *continental climate*. The south is a little warmer and wetter than the north, which is why peaches grow there and not near Chicago.

Spring in Illinois brings *tornadoes*. Warm, wet air from the Gulf of Mexico crashes into cold, dry air from the north. The two twist together. A spinning funnel of wind can drop from a storm cloud. The worst tornado in United States history struck in 1925. It tore across Missouri, Illinois and Indiana in one afternoon. It killed about seven hundred people. Most of them were in southern Illinois towns like Murphysboro.

Rivers bring *floods*. In the wet summer of 1993, the Mississippi and Illinois rivers rose over their banks for weeks. Water covered farms and towns. Today, towns build tall earthen walls called levees along rivers. Schools practice tornado drills. Knowing the weather is part of living in Illinois.

words.d: weather far from an ocean, with hot summers and cold winters
a spinning funnel of wind that drops from a storm cloud
when a river rises over its banks and covers the land
a wall of earth built along a river to hold back floods

look.title: The Sky Turns Green
look.text: It is a warm April afternoon in a small town in central Illinois. The air feels heavy and still. The sky to the west turns a strange greenish gray. Then the town's siren begins to wail. In the school, the teacher says one word, and every student walks quickly to the inside hallway and crouches by the wall.
look.prompt: What is happening? Why is an inside hallway with no windows the safest place?

check.q: Why does Illinois have hot summers and cold winters?
choices: It is very close to an ocean
It is far from any ocean, so nothing steadies the weather
It is near the South Pole
check.why: Land far from the sea heats up and cools down fast. This is called a continental climate.

check.q: What makes tornadoes form in spring?
choices: Warm wet air from the south crashing into cold dry air from the north
check.why: When warm, moist air and cold, dry air meet and twist, a funnel can drop from the storm cloud.

check.q: What is a levee for?
check.why: A levee is a wall of earth along a river that keeps high water off the land.

lessons.title: Soil, Coal and Water
lessons.mainIdea: The most valuable natural resources in Illinois are its soil, its coal and its water.
reading: A *natural resource* is something from nature that people use. The most valuable one in Illinois is not gold or oil. It is dirt. The deep black topsoil left by the prairie makes Illinois one of the best places on Earth to grow food. Farmland covers about three fourths of the state.

Under the soil lies *coal*. Coal is a black rock. It formed from swamp plants that were buried and squeezed for millions of years. It burns hot. People used it to heat homes and to make electricity. Illinois has some of the largest coal deposits in the country. Most of it lies under the central and southern parts of the state. Coal mining gave many towns their jobs. But burning coal dirties the air. So less coal is mined today than in the past.

Water is the third great resource. Lake Michigan gives drinking water to Chicago and its suburbs. Rivers carry barges and water the fields. Under the ground, layers of sand and gravel left by the glaciers hold water. Towns pump it up through wells. Rich soil, coal and water: the glaciers and the prairie gave Illinois all three.

words.d: something from nature that people use, like soil, water or coal
a black rock that burns, made from plants buried long ago
a deep hole dug to reach water underground

look.title: Three Jobs, One State
look.text: Maria's grandfather worked in a coal mine near Carbondale in the south. Her mother runs a farm near Bloomington in the center of the state. Maria's aunt works at the water plant in Chicago that cleans lake water for the city.
look.prompt: Which natural resource does each person's job depend on? Which resource will still be there in a thousand years, and which could run out?

check.q: Where did coal come from?
choices: Swamp plants buried and squeezed for millions of years
check.why: Coal formed from ancient plants that were buried under the ground and pressed for a very long time.

check.q: Why is less coal mined in Illinois today than in the past?
choices: It is too hard to reach
check.why: Illinois still has large coal deposits, but burning coal pollutes, so people use less of it.

check.q: How do many Illinois towns far from the lake get water?
choices: They ship it from the ocean
They pump it from underground through wells
check.why: Sand and gravel left by glaciers hold water underground. Towns reach it with wells.

lessons.title: Corn and Soybeans
lessons.mainIdea: Illinois farms grow corn and soybeans that feed animals and people around the world.
reading: Look out the window on a drive across Illinois in August. Row after row of tall green *corn*. Then a lower, bushier field of *soybeans*. Then corn again. These two crops cover most of the farmland in the state. Illinois is usually one of the top two states in the country for both, along with Iowa.

Very little of that corn is the sweet corn you eat off the cob. Most is field corn. It feeds cows, pigs and chickens. It is ground into cornmeal and corn syrup. Some is turned into a fuel called ethanol and mixed into gasoline. Soybeans are crushed for oil and for protein-rich animal feed. Both crops are shipped by train and barge, down the Mississippi to the port at New Orleans, and on to countries around the world.

Farming has changed. In 1900, most families in Illinois lived on farms and worked with horses. Today one farmer with a giant machine can plant or *harvest* hundreds of acres in a day. Fewer than one in fifty Illinoisans farms now. But the state still grows food for millions of people who have never seen a cornfield.

words.d: a tall grain plant; most Illinois corn feeds animals or becomes fuel or syrup
a bushy bean plant grown for oil and animal feed
to gather a crop when it is ripe

look.title: What Illinois Farmland Grows
look.unit: acres in a typical recent year, rounded
look.prompt: Corn and soybeans together cover about twenty million acres. About how many acres of wheat would fit in that space?

check.q: What happens to most Illinois corn?
choices: It is eaten fresh off the cob
It feeds animals or becomes syrup or fuel
It is used to build houses
check.why: Most is field corn, which feeds cows, pigs and chickens or is made into corn syrup and ethanol.

check.q: How does Illinois grain reach other countries?
choices: It does not leave the state
By train and barge down the Mississippi to New Orleans, then by ship
check.why: Barges carry grain down the river to the port at New Orleans, where ships take it overseas.

check.q: How has farming changed since 1900?
choices: Far fewer people farm, and big machines do the work
More people farm now than before
check.why: In 1900 most families farmed with horses. Today fewer than one in fifty Illinoisans farms, using big machines.

lessons.title: People Change the Land
lessons.mainIdea: People have reshaped Illinois by draining, plowing, building and even turning a river around.
reading: The land shapes people, but people also shape the land. Much of the Illinois prairie was wet and swampy in spring. Farmers dug ditches and buried clay pipes called *drain tiles* to carry the water away. Thousands of miles of them still run under the fields. Without them, much of central Illinois could not be farmed.

Chicago made the biggest change of all. The Chicago River used to flow into Lake Michigan. It carried the city's waste into its own drinking water. People got sick. So engineers dug a deep canal. In 1900 they made the river flow backward, away from the lake and toward the Mississippi. Chicago also filled in part of the lake to build parks. It even raised whole streets out of the mud.

Every change has a cost. Draining the wetlands took away homes for ducks and fish. Plowing the prairie erased it. Coal mines left scars. Today people work to *restore* some of what was lost, replanting prairie and cleaning rivers. The question for your generation is how to use the land and still take care of it.

words.d: a buried pipe that carries water away from wet farmland
a waterway dug by people for boats or for moving water
to bring something back to the way it was

look.title: A Settler Describes the Wet Prairie
look.text: A writer who lived in Illinois in the 1830s described the spring prairie as a place where the ground shook under a horse's feet and water stood in every low spot, so that travelers rode for miles with the horses' legs in water and the air full of biting flies.
look.cite: Eliza Farnham, Life in Prairie Land, 1846, paraphrased
look.prompt: What problem did farmers have to solve before they could plant this land? How did they solve it?

check.q: What did Chicago do to its river in 1900?
choices: Made it flow backward, away from the lake
Made it flow into Lake Michigan
check.why: Engineers dug a canal so the river carried waste away from the lake and toward the Mississippi.

check.q: Why did Chicago reverse its river?
choices: The river was carrying waste into the city's drinking water
check.why: The river dumped waste into the lake, where the city got its water, and people got sick.

check.q: What is one cost of draining the wetlands?
choices: Ducks and fish lost their homes
check.why: Every change has a cost. Wet places that animals needed were turned into fields.

review.q: Which of these is NOT a neighbor of Illinois?
review.why: Illinois borders Wisconsin, Iowa, Missouri, Kentucky and Indiana. Ohio is farther east.

review.q: Which river forms the southern border of Illinois?
review.why: The Ohio River separates Illinois from Kentucky and joins the Mississippi at Cairo.

review.q: Why is most of Illinois flat?
choices: Glaciers scraped it flat during the Ice Age
It was once the bottom of Lake Michigan
review.why: Ice sheets more than a mile thick ground down hills and filled valleys.

review.q: What made the topsoil of Illinois so rich?
choices: Thousands of years of prairie grass rotting into the ground
review.why: Prairie plants and their deep roots died and regrew for thousands of years, building deep black soil.

review.q: Where do about two thirds of Illinoisans live?
review.why: The Chicago area, in the northern region, holds most of the state's people.

review.q: What kind of weather danger comes when warm Gulf air meets cold northern air?
review.why: The clash of warm, wet air and cold, dry air can twist into a tornado.

review.q: Which three natural resources does the chapter call the most valuable in Illinois?
review.why: Rich soil, large coal deposits and plentiful water are the state's key resources.

review.q: What is one way people changed the land of Illinois?
choices: They built mountains in the south
They made the Chicago River flow backward
review.why: In 1900 engineers reversed the Chicago River so waste flowed away from the city's drinking water.

chapters.title: Illinois Then and Now
chapters.bigQuestion: How did Illinois change from a land of mound cities and prairie into the state we live in today?

story.title: The Night the Wind Changed
story.kicker: Chicago, October 1871. From a rooftop, a girl watches a red glow in the southwest grow bigger, and the wind turns toward her.
paragraphs: It is Sunday night, the eighth of October, 1871. A twelve-year-old girl named Clara climbs onto the roof of her family's wooden house on the North Side of Chicago. All summer it has barely rained. The city is built of wood: wooden houses, wooden sidewalks, even wooden streets. Everything is dry as paper. To the southwest, the sky glows orange.

A fire has started in a barn on DeKoven Street. Nobody knows exactly how. Later, people will tell a story about a cow kicking over a lantern, but no one ever proves it. What matters is the wind. It is blowing hard from the southwest, straight toward the heart of the city. Sparks fly ahead of the flames. They land on roofs blocks away and start new fires.

By midnight the fire jumps the Chicago River. People said a river would stop it. It does not. Clara's father calls her down from the roof. The family grabs what they can: a Bible, a quilt, a box of papers. They join a crowd pushing north and east toward the lake. Behind them the courthouse bell rings and rings, and then the bell tower falls.

The fire burns all of Monday. Then, late on Monday night, it begins to rain. By Tuesday morning the fire is out. About three hundred people are dead. Close to one hundred thousand have no home. Clara's house is a square of ashes. The downtown is gone.

But something else happens in the ashes. Within a week, people are building again. Trains bring lumber and bricks and food from all over the country. Within twenty years, Chicago has the tallest buildings in the world and more than a million people. The fire is the worst thing that ever happened to the city, and, in a strange way, the start of its greatest years.
story.think: Clara's family had a few minutes to grab what they could carry. What would you take? Why did people rebuild instead of leaving?

lessons.title: The City of Mounds
lessons.mainIdea: A thousand years ago, Cahokia near today's St. Louis was the largest city north of Mexico.
reading: Stand at the top of Monks Mound in southern Illinois. It is a hill of earth about one hundred feet tall. Its flat top is bigger than a football field. People built it by hand, basket by basket, more than nine hundred years ago. Around it once stood more than a hundred smaller *mounds*, a great plaza and thousands of houses. This was *Cahokia*, the largest city north of Mexico in its time.

Cahokia was busiest around the year 1100. Archaeologists, who study the past by digging up what people left behind, think ten to twenty thousand people lived there. Farmers grew corn, squash and beans on the rich river bottomland. Traders brought seashells from the Gulf of Mexico and copper from Lake Superior. A circle of tall wooden posts marked the sunrise on the first day of each season.

By about 1350, the people of Cahokia had left. No one is sure why. Floods, dry years, wars, or worn-out land may all have played a part. We know about Cahokia only from what is left in the ground: pots, tools, house posts, and the mounds themselves. Today it is a state historic site and a World Heritage Site, and you can climb Monks Mound yourself.

words.d: a hill of earth built by people, used for temples, homes or burials
a great mound city near the Mississippi River that was busiest around the year 1100
a scientist who learns about the past by digging up what people left behind

look.title: Monks Mound by the Numbers
look.cite: Cahokia Mounds State Historic Site, rounded
look.prompt: The mound was built one basket of dirt at a time. What does its size tell you about how many people worked on it and how they were organized?

check.q: How was Monks Mound built?
choices: By people carrying earth in baskets
check.why: People built it by hand, basket by basket, over many years.

check.q: How do we know about the people of Cahokia?
choices: From what archaeologists dig up: pots, tools, posts and mounds
check.why: The people of Cahokia left no writing. Everything we know comes from what remains in the ground.

check.q: What happened to Cahokia by about 1350?
choices: The people had left, for reasons no one is sure of
The French built a fort there
It burned down in a great fire
check.why: The city was empty by around 1350. Floods, drought, war or worn-out land may have played a part.

lessons.title: The Illinois People
lessons.mainIdea: The state is named for the Illinois, a group of related nations who lived along its rivers.
reading: French explorers paddled down the Mississippi in 1673. They met people who lived in large villages along the rivers. These were the *Illinois*, also called the Illiniwek or Inoka. They were not one tribe but several related nations. The Peoria, the Kaskaskia and the Cahokia were among them. The French wrote their name down as Illinois, and the land took that name.

The Illinois lived in long houses covered with woven mats, in villages that could hold thousands of people. In summer, women grew corn, beans and squash. In winter, families spread out to hunt bison and deer. They traded with other nations along the rivers, and they were known for their long journeys.

The 1700s were hard for the Illinois. Diseases from Europe, which they had never met before, killed many. Wars with other nations killed more. By the early 1800s, most of the Illinois people had been pushed out of the state, and in 1832 the last remaining tribes were forced to move west. Today their *descendants* belong to the Peoria Tribe of Indians of Oklahoma.

words.d: a group of related Native nations, including the Peoria and Kaskaskia, for whom the state is named
a person who comes from a family or people that lived before

look.title: A French Priest Meets the Illinois, 1673
look.text: Father Jacques Marquette wrote in his journal that when he and his companions came to an Illinois village, an old man met them at the door of his lodge, held his hands up toward the sun, and told them how good it was that they had come. The people then fed them and gave them a peace pipe as a sign of safe passage.
look.cite: Jacques Marquette, journal of the 1673 voyage, paraphrased
look.prompt: This is the French side of the story. What might the Illinois villagers have been thinking as they watched these strangers arrive?

check.q: Which of these was one of the Illinois nations?
check.why: The Peoria, Kaskaskia and Cahokia were among the related nations that made up the Illinois.

check.q: What did Illinois families do in winter?
choices: Spread out to hunt bison and deer
check.why: In summer they farmed in villages. In winter they broke into smaller groups to hunt.

check.q: Why did the Illinois people become fewer in the 1700s?
choices: Diseases from Europe and wars killed many
check.why: New diseases and wars with other nations killed many, and later the survivors were forced west.

lessons.title: French Forts and Fur Traders
lessons.mainIdea: For about a century, French traders and soldiers lived along the Illinois rivers, trading for furs.
reading: The first Europeans in Illinois were not farmers. They were French. In 1673, a priest named Jacques Marquette and a mapmaker named Louis Jolliet paddled down the Mississippi and back up the Illinois River. They were looking for a route to the sea. A few years later, an explorer named La Salle built a fort near today's Peoria.

What the French wanted most was *fur*. Beaver fur made the best hats in Europe, and a hat could sell for a lot of money. French *traders* paddled canoes deep into the country. They traded metal pots, cloth, knives and guns to Native hunters for beaver and deer skins. Many traders married Native women, and their children grew up speaking both languages.

The French built small towns and forts along the Mississippi: Kaskaskia, Cahokia and the stone Fort de Chartres. Priests built churches. Farmers grew wheat. But France lost a war with Britain in 1763 and gave up the land. The British held it briefly. Then, during the American Revolution, a Virginian named George Rogers Clark captured Kaskaskia in 1778, and Illinois became American.

words.d: the thick hair of an animal like a beaver, used for hats and coats
a person who exchanges goods with others to make a living
a strong building with walls where soldiers live and guard a place

look.title: A Trade on the Riverbank
look.text: A French trader pulls his canoe onto the shore near an Illinois village. He unrolls a blanket and lays out a copper kettle, a steel knife and a bolt of red cloth. A hunter sets down a stack of beaver pelts. They talk, half in French, half in Illinois, with hand signs. Both walk away with something they could not make themselves.
look.prompt: What did each side get from the trade? Why might a steel knife be worth a lot to someone who has never had one?

check.q: Who explored the Mississippi and Illinois rivers in 1673?
check.why: The priest Jacques Marquette and the mapmaker Louis Jolliet made the trip looking for a route to the sea.

check.q: What did Native hunters get in trade for furs?
choices: Metal pots, cloth, knives and guns
check.why: The French traded metal tools, cloth and weapons that Native people could not make themselves.

check.q: How did Illinois become American?
choices: The French sold it to Chicago
The Illinois people gave it away
George Rogers Clark captured Kaskaskia in 1778
check.why: During the Revolution, Clark took the old French town of Kaskaskia from the British, and Illinois became part of the new United States.

lessons.title: The Twenty-First State
lessons.mainIdea: Illinois became a state in 1818, when it was mostly empty prairie with a few thousand settlers.
reading: On December 3, 1818, Illinois became the twenty-first state of the United States. It was a small, quiet place. Only about thirty-five thousand people lived in the whole state, most of them in the far south near the rivers. Chicago did not exist yet. The first *capital* was the old French town of Kaskaskia, on the Mississippi.

Settlers came down the Ohio River on flatboats from Kentucky, Tennessee and Virginia. Later they came overland from New York and New England. They built log cabins, cleared land and planted corn. They argued about *slavery*. Illinois entered as a free state, but for years some people were still held as slaves there, and Black residents had few rights.

As the state filled up, the capital moved north, first to Vandalia in 1820 and then to Springfield in 1839. A young lawmaker named Abraham Lincoln helped push for the move to Springfield. By 1850 Illinois had more than eight hundred thousand people. The empty prairie was filling fast.

words.d: the city where a state's government meets and works
owning people and forcing them to work without pay or freedom
a person who moves to a new place to live and farm

look.title: How Illinois Grew
look.prompt: Between which two dates did the state grow the most? What do you think brought so many people?

check.q: When did Illinois become a state?
check.why: Illinois became the twenty-first state on December 3, 1818.

check.q: Where was the first state capital?
check.why: Kaskaskia, an old French town on the Mississippi, was the first capital. The capital later moved to Vandalia and then Springfield.

check.q: How did many early settlers reach Illinois?
choices: On flatboats down the Ohio River
check.why: Families floated down the Ohio from Kentucky, Tennessee and Virginia with everything they owned.

lessons.title: Canals Connect the Waters
lessons.mainIdea: Canals linked the Great Lakes to the East and to the Mississippi, and turned Chicago into a trading center.
reading: Before trains, the cheapest way to move heavy things was by water. But the Great Lakes did not connect to the East Coast or to the Mississippi. So people dug *canals*, long ditches of water that boats could travel. In 1825, New York finished the Erie Canal. It linked Lake Erie to the Hudson River and New York City. Now a boat could go from Chicago all the way to the ocean.

Illinois built its own canal. Workers dug the Illinois and Michigan Canal from Chicago to the Illinois River, about ninety-six miles. Thousands of the diggers were Irish immigrants who worked with shovels and wheelbarrows. The canal opened in 1848. Now grain from Illinois farms could float to Chicago, across the lakes, through the Erie Canal, and on to New York.

The canals changed everything. Farmers could sell corn and wheat far away. Lumber from Michigan forests came to Chicago to build houses. Chicago, which had only a few hundred people in 1830, grew into a busy town of *warehouses*, docks and grain elevators. The canal made Chicago the place where the East met the West.

words.d: a long, narrow waterway dug by people so boats can travel on it
a person who moves to a new country to live
a big building where goods are stored before they are sold or shipped

look.title: A Sack of Wheat Goes East
look.text: A farmer near Ottawa, Illinois, loads sacks of wheat onto a canal boat pulled by mules. The boat creeps to Chicago. There the wheat is poured into a tall grain elevator, then into a lake ship. The ship crosses Lake Michigan, Lake Huron and Lake Erie. At Buffalo the wheat goes onto an Erie Canal boat, then down the Hudson River to New York City, then onto a ship for England.
look.prompt: Count how many times the wheat changed boats. Why was this still cheaper than carrying it by wagon?

check.q: What did the Erie Canal connect?
choices: Lake Erie and the Hudson River, and so New York City
Lake Michigan and the Illinois River
check.why: The Erie Canal, finished in 1825, linked the Great Lakes to the Hudson and the ocean.

check.q: Who dug much of the Illinois and Michigan Canal?
check.why: Thousands of Irish immigrants dug the ninety-six-mile canal by hand. It opened in 1848.

check.q: Why did canals help Chicago grow?
choices: They brought fresh water to the city
Goods from farms and forests could be shipped through Chicago to faraway markets
check.why: With the canals, Chicago became the meeting point between the farms of the West and the cities of the East.

lessons.title: Railroads Cross the Prairie
lessons.mainIdea: Railroads made Chicago the nation's biggest rail center and let towns and farms spread across the prairie.
reading: Canals froze in winter and moved slowly. Trains did not. In the 1850s, *railroads* raced across Illinois. The Illinois Central, finished in 1856, ran the whole length of the state, about seven hundred miles. For a while it was the longest railroad in the world. Along its tracks, the railroad company sold land to settlers and planted new towns every few miles.

Rails were laid on top of the flat prairie, so building was fast and cheap. Trains carried corn, hogs and cattle to Chicago and carried plows, cloth and lumber back out. A trip that took a week by wagon took a day by train. Towns that got a station grew. Towns that did not often died.

Chicago became the center of the web. By 1860 more than ten rail lines met there. The city built enormous *stockyards* where cattle and hogs from across the West were sold and turned into meat, then shipped east in ice-cooled railroad cars. By 1890 Chicago had more than a million people. Only New York was bigger.

words.d: a track of steel rails that trains run on, and the company that runs them
a huge set of pens where cattle and hogs are kept and sold

look.title: The Depot
look.text: It is 1870 in a new town on the Illinois Central line. The town is only twelve years old. The depot sits by the tracks. Next to it stands a grain elevator, then a lumber yard, a hotel and a general store. Twice a day a train stops. Farmers pull up with wagons of corn. A boy waits for a package from Chicago.
look.prompt: Why did the grain elevator, hotel and store all cluster near the tracks? What would happen to this town if the trains stopped coming?

check.q: What was special about the Illinois Central in 1856?
choices: It was the first train in the world
It was the longest railroad in the world at the time
check.why: It ran about seven hundred miles, the whole length of the state, longer than any railroad then.

check.q: What happened to a prairie town that got a rail station?
check.why: A station meant farmers could ship crops and stores could get goods. Towns without one often faded.

check.q: What did the Chicago stockyards do?
choices: Sold cattle and hogs and turned them into meat for shipping
check.why: Animals from across the West came by train to the stockyards, and meat went east in ice-cooled cars.

lessons.title: From Fort to City
lessons.mainIdea: Chicago grew from a swampy trading post and a small fort into a big city in only a few decades.
reading: The place where the Chicago River meets Lake Michigan was once a muddy marsh. Its name comes from a Native word for the wild onion or garlic that grew there. The first non-Native settler was a trader named Jean Baptiste Point du Sable. He was a Black man of African and French background. He built a farm and trading post there in the 1780s.

In 1803, the United States Army built *Fort Dearborn* at the river mouth to guard the spot. Chicago became a town in 1833. It had about three hundred and fifty people. The Potawatomi, who lived in the area, signed a treaty that same year. They were forced to give up their land and move west. The town they left behind grew wildly.

The canal, and then the railroads, did the rest. By 1860 Chicago had more than one hundred thousand people. Immigrants arrived from Germany, Ireland, Sweden and Poland to build, dig and work in factories. By 1870 the *population* was about three hundred thousand. Then came the fire.

words.d: the army fort built in 1803 where the Chicago River meets Lake Michigan
the number of people who live in a place
a written agreement between nations, often about land

look.title: Chicago Grows
look.prompt: In which twenty-year stretch did the city grow the most? What happened in those years to bring so many people?

check.q: What was Fort Dearborn?
choices: An army fort built in 1803 at the mouth of the Chicago River
check.why: The United States Army built Fort Dearborn to guard the spot where the river met the lake.

check.q: What happened to the Potawatomi in 1833?
choices: They were forced by treaty to give up their land and move west
They became the first city council
check.why: In the same year Chicago became a town, the Potawatomi signed a treaty giving up their land and were moved west.

check.q: About how many people lived in Chicago in 1870?
check.why: The city had grown from a few hundred people in 1833 to roughly three hundred thousand by 1870.

lessons.title: The Great Fire and After
lessons.mainIdea: The fire of 1871 destroyed the heart of Chicago, and the rebuilt city invented the skyscraper.
reading: On October 8, 1871, after a long dry summer, a fire started in a barn on the West Side of Chicago. A strong wind pushed it northeast into the heart of the city. Wooden buildings, wooden sidewalks and wooden streets fed it. It jumped the river. It burned for two days. About three hundred people died. About one hundred thousand lost their homes. Roughly seventeen thousand buildings were gone.

Then the city started over. Help came by train from across the country: food, blankets, money and lumber. New laws said downtown buildings had to be made of brick, stone or iron instead of wood. Builders tried new ideas. In 1885, the Home Insurance Building went up with a frame of steel holding up its walls. Many people call it the first *skyscraper*.

Twenty-two years after the fire, in 1893, Chicago hosted a world's fair to show off. Millions of visitors came to see white palaces, electric lights and the first Ferris wheel. Chicago had gone from ashes to one of the great cities of the world. The fire had cleared the way.

words.d: a very tall building held up by a frame of steel
a giant show where countries and companies display new inventions and art

look.title: A Survivor Remembers
look.text: One woman who lived through the fire later wrote that the streets were so bright from the flames that she could read a newspaper at midnight, that the wind carried burning boards over her head, and that thousands of people stood in the lake up to their waists to escape the heat.
look.cite: Chicago fire survivors' accounts published in the 1870s, paraphrased
look.prompt: Why is a survivor's account useful to historians? What might a survivor remember wrong or leave out?

check.q: What new rule did Chicago make after the fire?
choices: Downtown buildings must be brick, stone or iron, not wood
Everyone must move to the suburbs
check.why: The city banned wooden buildings downtown so a fire could not spread the same way again.

check.q: What made the Home Insurance Building of 1885 special?
choices: It was the first building in Chicago
A steel frame held up its walls, so it could be very tall
It was a world's fair palace
check.why: A steel frame carried the weight instead of thick walls. Many call it the first skyscraper.

check.q: What did the 1893 world's fair show the world?
choices: That Chicago was still in ruins
That Chicago had moved to Springfield
That Chicago had rebuilt into a great city
check.why: Only twenty-two years after the fire, millions came to see the fair's palaces, lights and Ferris wheel.

lessons.title: The Great Migration
lessons.mainIdea: In the 1900s, hundreds of thousands of Black Americans moved from the South to Chicago for jobs and freedom.
reading: In 1916, a young man in Mississippi read a copy of the Chicago Defender, a Black newspaper that friends passed hand to hand. It said Chicago had jobs in steel mills and stockyards that paid real wages. It said Black people could vote there and send their children to school. He bought a train ticket north. Millions made the same choice. Historians call it the *Great Migration*.

Why leave? In the South, laws kept Black people from voting, from good schools and from most good jobs. Violence was common and the law did not protect them. In the North, factories needed workers during World War One. Chicago's Black population grew from about forty-four thousand in 1910 to more than two hundred thousand by 1930.

Chicago was not a promised land. Many landlords would rent to Black families only in one part of the South Side, so housing was crowded and cost too much. In 1919, a fight at a beach turned into a week of riots that killed dozens of people, most of them Black. Still, migrants built churches, businesses, newspapers and music. The blues came up the river from Mississippi and became Chicago blues. The *neighborhood* called Bronzeville became a center of Black life in America.

words.d: the move of millions of Black Americans from the South to northern cities in the 1900s
a person who moves from one region to another to live
a part of a city where people live near each other

look.title: Two Letters
look.text: A letter from Chicago, 1917: I work at a steel mill and get paid every week. My boy goes to a school with a library. Nobody makes me step off the sidewalk. A letter back from Mississippi: Rent there sounds high. Cousin says it snows for months. But send the train fare and we will come.
look.prompt: What pulled people to Chicago? What pushed them out of the South? What did they give up?

check.q: What was the Great Migration?
choices: Immigrants coming from Germany and Ireland
Black Americans moving from the South to northern cities
check.why: In the 1900s, millions of Black Americans left the South for cities like Chicago.

check.q: What problem did Black families often face in Chicago?
choices: Landlords would rent to them only in one crowded part of the city
The trains would not carry them
check.why: Housing was limited to certain areas, so it was crowded and expensive, and in 1919 riots broke out.

check.q: What is one thing migrants built in Chicago?
choices: Churches, businesses, newspapers and a new kind of music
check.why: Migrants built a rich community life in Bronzeville, including Chicago blues.

lessons.title: Cities, Farms and Universities
lessons.mainIdea: Illinois today mixes a world city, deep farmland, big universities and people from everywhere.
reading: Illinois today has about twelve million eight hundred thousand people. It is one of the six biggest states. Chicago is still the center, with about two point seven million people. Its airport is one of the busiest in the world. Its tall towers, trains, museums and lake parks draw visitors from everywhere. About one in every five Illinoisans was born in another country. In Chicago you can hear more than a hundred languages.

Outside the city, Illinois still feeds the world. Its farms grow more corn and soybeans than almost any other state. Trucks, trains and barges carry grain from small towns to ports and factories. The state also makes machines, medicines and food products, and Chicago is a center for banks and trading.

Illinois is also a place of learning. The University of Illinois in Urbana and Champaign, founded in 1867, is one of the largest *universities* in the country. Scientists there helped invent early computers and the web browser. The University of Chicago, Northwestern and many others bring students from around the world. Springfield remains the capital, where the state's laws are made.

words.d: a school where people study after high school and where scientists do research
a place where ships load and unload goods

look.title: One Day, Three Illinoisans
look.text: At six in the morning, a farmer near Decatur climbs into a combine to harvest soybeans. At the same hour, a nurse in Chicago gets off the night shift at a hospital and rides the train home past the skyline. At the University of Illinois, a student from India walks to a computer lab to work on a project.
look.prompt: How are these three lives connected? What does each depend on from the others?

check.q: About what share of Illinoisans were born in another country?
check.why: Roughly one in five people in Illinois is an immigrant, and Chicago is home to speakers of more than a hundred languages.

check.q: When was the University of Illinois founded?
check.why: The University of Illinois in Urbana and Champaign opened in 1867 and is now one of the largest in the country.

check.q: Which of these does Illinois still do today?
choices: Grow more corn and soybeans than almost any other state
Send all its people to Chicago
check.why: Farms remain a huge part of Illinois. The state is usually first or second in corn and soybeans.

lessons.title: Lincoln, Addams and Wells
lessons.mainIdea: Three Illinoisans, Abraham Lincoln, Jane Addams and Ida B. Wells, used words and action to make the country fairer.
reading: Abraham Lincoln moved to Illinois at twenty-one, in 1830. He split rails, ran a store, and taught himself law from borrowed books. He became a lawyer in Springfield and a lawmaker. In 1858 he warned that the country could not stay half slave and half free. In 1860 he was elected president. He led the nation through the Civil War, and in 1863 he declared enslaved people in the rebel states free. He was shot in 1865, and a train carried him home to Springfield.

Jane Addams grew up in Cedarville, in northern Illinois. In 1889 she moved into a rundown mansion on Halsted Street in Chicago, in a neighborhood full of poor immigrants, and opened *Hull House*. It offered a kindergarten, English classes, a gym, art and a place to be heard. Addams fought for safer factories, laws against child labor and cleaner streets. In 1931 she won the Nobel Peace Prize.

Ida B. Wells was born enslaved in Mississippi in 1862. She became a teacher and then a *journalist*. When a mob murdered her friends in Memphis, she wrote the truth about lynching and printed it, though her office was destroyed and her life threatened. She moved to Chicago in the 1890s, helped found groups for civil rights and women's votes, and never stopped writing. Chicago named a major street for her in 2019.

words.d: the settlement house Jane Addams opened in Chicago in 1889 to help poor immigrant neighbors
a person who finds out facts and writes news for the public
the murder of a person by a mob, outside the law

look.title: A House Divided, 1858
look.text: A house divided against itself cannot stand. I believe this government cannot endure, permanently half slave and half free.
look.cite: Abraham Lincoln, speech in Springfield, Illinois, June 1858
look.prompt: Lincoln borrowed the picture of a house from the Bible. Why is a house a good picture for a country? What did he think had to happen?

check.q: What did Lincoln do before he became president?
choices: He was a lawyer and lawmaker in Springfield
He was a newspaper editor in Chicago
check.why: Lincoln taught himself law, practiced in Springfield and served as a lawmaker before winning the presidency in 1860.

check.q: What was Hull House?
choices: A fort on the Chicago River
A house in a poor Chicago neighborhood where Jane Addams offered classes and help
check.why: Addams opened Hull House in 1889 to serve immigrant neighbors with a kindergarten, classes and more.

check.q: What did all three of these people have in common?
choices: They used words and action to make the country fairer
They were all born in Illinois
They all lived in the same century as Cahokia
check.why: Lincoln, Addams and Wells each spoke out and worked for freedom and fairness. Only Addams was born in Illinois.

lessons.title: Two Presidents from Illinois
lessons.mainIdea: Ronald Reagan and Barack Obama, two presidents with very different ideas, both started out in Illinois.
reading: Ronald Reagan was born in 1911 in the small town of Tampico, Illinois, and grew up in Dixon, on the Rock River. As a teenager he worked as a lifeguard. He went to Eureka College in central Illinois, then became a radio sports announcer and a movie actor in California. He was elected governor of California, and in 1980 he was elected *president*. He served two terms, from 1981 to 1989.

Barack Obama was born in Hawaii in 1961. After college he moved to Chicago to work as a community organizer on the South Side. He helped neighbors push for better housing and jobs. He taught law at the University of Chicago. He served in the Illinois state senate in Springfield. In 2004 Illinois voters sent him to the United States Senate. In 2008 he was elected president, the first Black president. He gave his victory speech in Chicago's Grant Park. He served from 2009 to 2017.

The two men belonged to different *political parties*. They disagreed about how big government should be and what it should do. Reagan argued for lower taxes and fewer government rules. Obama argued for government help with health care and jobs. Americans still argue about both. But both men learned about people and politics in Illinois towns and neighborhoods first.

check.q: Where was Ronald Reagan born?

review.q: What was the largest city north of Mexico around the year 1100?
review.why: Cahokia, a mound city near today's St. Louis, held ten to twenty thousand people.

review.q: Why did the French come to Illinois in the 1600s and 1700s?
review.why: French traders wanted beaver furs for hats and traded metal goods and cloth for them.

review.q: In what year did Illinois become a state?
review.why: Illinois became the twenty-first state on December 3, 1818.

review.q: Which two things made Chicago a great trading center in the 1800s?
review.why: The Illinois and Michigan Canal and then the railroads made Chicago the meeting point of East and West.

review.q: What happened in Chicago in October 1871?
choices: A great fire destroyed the heart of the city
review.why: After a dry summer, a wind-driven fire burned for two days and left about a hundred thousand people homeless.

review.q: Why did many Black Americans move to Chicago during the Great Migration?
choices: For jobs, schools and the right to vote
Because the South was too cold
review.why: The North offered factory jobs and rights that laws in the South denied to Black people.

review.q: Who opened Hull House in Chicago in 1889?
review.why: Jane Addams opened Hull House on Halsted Street to serve poor immigrant neighbors.

review.q: Which two presidents started out in Illinois?
review.why: Abraham Lincoln, Ronald Reagan and Barack Obama all lived and worked in Illinois before becoming president.
